newsitem.title: UK: UK court backs Equitas 'pay now sue later' clause.
newsitem.headline: UK court backs Equitas 'pay now sue later' clause.

text.p: Lloyd's of London on Thursday welcomed a decision by the British High Court which it said would mean members who had not paid their premiums to reinsurance vehicle Equitas, would have to do so before they could sue the insurance merket.

Lloyd's said in a statement that as a result of today's judgement they would be able to obtain summary judgements against members who have refused to pay and have alleged that they were induced to join Lloyd's by fraudulent misrepresentation.
Equitas was set up to run-off the market's huge pre-1993 losses, an integral part of the recovery plans implemented by Lloyd's last year.
It allowed a line to be drawn under the eight billion pounds ($13 billion) of losses accumulated between 1988 and 1993 which at one point threatened to sink Lloyd's.

The defendants in the test case had claimed they had been victims of fraud by Lloyd's and were entitled to set aside membership and refuse to pay the Equitas premiums until their claims for damages had been determined.
But Mr Justice Colman said that they were not entitled to rescind their contracts with Lloyd's.

"The defendants are by clause 5.5 of the Equitas contract precluded from setting off their counter-claim for damages for fraud against Lloyd's claim for the Equitas premium. The defendants are not entitled to a stay of execution of a judgement against them for the Equitas premium," he said.
Other defences advanced by the members to prevent recovery of the Equitas premiums were rejected by the court in February.
Those had argued that non-accepting members had not been validly bound into the Equitas scheme and so were not liable to pay the Equitas premium.

"Lloyd's is delighted that today's ruling, taken together with Mr Justice Colman's earlier ruling in the action, upholds the legal basis for the reinsurance into Equitas and allows Lloyd's to pursue, for the benefit of the members of the Society, those members who are yet to pay their Equitas premiums," said Lloyd's chief executive Ron Sandler.

Philip Holden, head of Lloyd's financial recovery department, said that over 1,300 writs for recovery of unpaid premiums had been issuesd and that Lloyd's would now begin taking steps to enforce them.
Lloyd's is seeking to recover around 350 million pounds from those 1,300.
The total number of non-acceptors is around 1,800.

"As far as Lloyd's is concerned this is the last defence that has been offered against our ability to collect money. If they now wish to carry on with these allegations of fraud they'll have to mount their own case," said a Lloyd's spokesman.
